title: Scientific Notation
short: Write numbers as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.
trouble: Students move the decimal point the wrong way for small numbers, or leave a first factor like 45 × 10³.

blocks.html: Light travels about 300,000,000 meters each second. A small bacterium can be about 0.000002 meter long. Numbers like these are easy to misread, because you have to count zeros. Scientific notation writes them as a short number times a power of 10: $3 \times 10^{8}$ and $2 \times 10^{-6}$.
It rests on multiplying and dividing by powers of 10: each factor of 10 moves every digit one place.
A number is in scientific notation when it is written as $a \times 10^{n}$, where $1 \le a < 10$ and $n$ is an integer. Big numbers get a positive $n$. Numbers between 0 and 1 get a negative $n$.

$3.08 \times 10^{6}$ multiplies 3.08 by 10 six times, which moves its digits six places to the left: 3,080,000. A negative exponent divides instead: $10^{-4} = \frac{1}{10{,}000}$, so $5.06 \times 10^{-4}$ moves the digits four places to the right: 0.000506.

blocks.title: A big number
steps: Put the decimal point after the first nonzero digit: $3.08$, which is between 1 and 10.
From 3.08 to 3,080,000 the point moves 6 places to the right.

blocks.title: A small number
steps: To get from 5.06 back to 0.000506, the point moves 4 places to the left, which is dividing by $10^{4}$.

blocks.title: Back to standard form
steps: A negative exponent: the number is less than 1.
Move the point 3 places left, filling with zeros.

blocks.html: Two common slips. (1) Using a positive exponent for a small number: $0.0045 = 4.5 \times 10^{3}$ is wrong, because $4.5 \times 10^{3}$ is 4,500. A number less than 1 needs a negative exponent: $4.5 \times 10^{-3}$. (2) Stopping at $45 \times 10^{3}$. It equals 45,000, but 45 is not less than 10. Move one more place: $4.5 \times 10^{4}$.
